title: Sampling & Probability Distributions
sub: Lecture 8 · sampling methods, discrete & continuous distributions
blurb: Sampling methods (with/without replacement, stratified, cluster), Binomial, Hypergeometric, Poisson, Normal, Standard Normal, and derived χ², t and F distributions.
lede: Before we infer anything about a population, we need to know how samples are drawn and which probability distributions govern counts and measurements. This lecture covers sampling designs, key discrete distributions (Binomial, Hypergeometric, Poisson), the Normal distribution with standardization, and derived distributions (χ², t, F).
six: In **simple random sampling**, every sample of size n is equally likely; **with replacement** gives independent trials, while **without replacement** gives dependent trials.
**Binomial** Bi(n, π) models successes in n independent trials (E(X) = nπ, Var(X) = nπ(1-π)); **Hypergeometric** Hy(N, M, n) models sampling without replacement.
When sample size is small relative to population (**n < 0.05N**), Hypergeometric Hy(N, M, n) can be approximated by Binomial Bi(n, π = M/N).
**Poisson** Po(λ) models occurrences in a continuous interval with E(X) = Var(X) = λ, and approximates Binomial when **π ≤ 0.1 and n > 30** (λ = nπ).
Any **Normal** variable X ~ N(μ, σ²) is standardized via **Z = (X - μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1)**, using Table I for F(z) and Table II for quantiles z_P (x_P = μ + σ·z_P).
For **Student's t(df)**, symmetry gives t_{1-P}(df) = -t_P(df) and df > 30 approximates Z; for **F(df₁, df₂)**, f_{1-P}(df₁, df₂) = 1 / f_P(df₂, df₁).

questions.q: How does sampling with replacement differ from sampling without replacement?
questions.h: Think about whether trial probabilities stay constant or change.
questions.answer: With replacement allows elements to be selected more than once (independent trials); without replacement allows at most once (dependent trials)
wrong: With replacement is only for continuous variables; without replacement is for discrete
With replacement gives dependent trials; without replacement gives independent trials
With replacement selects every 10th element; without replacement selects clusters
questions.e: Sampling with replacement keeps probabilities constant across trials (independent). Sampling without replacement changes probabilities after each draw (dependent).

questions.q: How do stratified sampling and cluster sampling differ?
questions.h: One samples from every subgroup; the other randomly picks whole subgroups.
questions.answer: Stratified divides into homogeneous strata and samples from every stratum; cluster randomly selects some clusters and surveys all elements in them
wrong: Stratified is less reliable than cluster sampling
Cluster sampling samples from every cluster; stratified picks only one cluster
Stratified selects every 10th element; cluster uses replacement
questions.e: Stratified sampling divides the population into homogeneous strata and samples from each stratum. Cluster sampling selects some clusters by SRS and uses all elements in them (less reliable than stratified).

questions.q: For a Binomial random variable X ~ Bi(n, π), what are its expected value E(X) and variance Var(X)?
questions.h: Multiply n by π, and for variance multiply by (1 - π).
questions.answer: E(X) = n·π and Var(X) = n·π·(1 - π)
wrong: E(X) = π and Var(X) = π·(1 - π)
E(X) = n/π and Var(X) = n·(1 - π)
questions.e: For X ~ Bi(n, π), E(X) = nπ and Var(X) = nπ(1 - π). When π = 0.5, the distribution is symmetric.

questions.q: Three cards are drawn WITH replacement from a 32-card deck (4 aces). What is the distribution of X (number of aces) and P(X = 1)?
questions.h: With replacement means independent trials with π = 4/32 = 1/8.
questions.e: With replacement, trials are independent with n = 3 and π = 4/32 = 1/8, so X ~ Bi(3, 1/8) and P(1) = 3·(1/8)·(49/64) ≈ 0.287.

questions.q: Three cards are drawn WITHOUT replacement from a 32-card deck (4 aces). Which distribution applies and what is P(X = 1)?
questions.h: Without replacement means dependent trials from a finite population N = 32.
questions.e: Sampling without replacement uses the Hypergeometric distribution Hy(N=32, M=4, n=3), giving C(4,1)·C(28,2)/C(32,3) ≈ 0.305.

questions.q: When can the Hypergeometric distribution Hy(N, M, n) be approximated by the Binomial distribution Bi(n, π = M/N)?
questions.h: The sample size n must be small compared to the population size N.
questions.e: If n < 0.05·N (sample is less than 5% of the population), Hy(N, M, n) is well approximated by Bi(n, M/N).

questions.q: What is a distinctive property of the expected value and variance of a Poisson random variable X ~ Po(λ)?
questions.h: Both depend on the single parameter λ > 0.
questions.answer: Both equal λ: E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ
questions.e: The Poisson distribution Po(λ) has a single parameter λ > 0 (average occurrences per interval), and both E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ.

questions.q: Under what conditions can a Binomial distribution Bi(n, π) be approximated by a Poisson distribution Po(λ = n·π)?
questions.h: Many trials and a small probability of success.
questions.e: When π ≤ 0.1 and n > 30, Bi(n, π) can be approximated by Po(λ) with λ = n·π (e.g., Bi(40, 0.05) ≈ Po(2)).

questions.q: Buses arrive at a stop at an average rate of 15 per hour. What is the probability that NO bus arrives within a 4-minute interval?
questions.h: Scale λ to 4 minutes (4/60 of an hour), then compute P(0) = e^(-λ)·λ⁰/0!.
questions.e: 15 buses per 60 minutes equals λ = 15·(4/60) = 1 bus per 4 minutes. Thus X ~ Po(1) and P(0) = e⁻¹·1⁰/0! = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368.

questions.q: When is the Normal distribution N(μ, σ²) generally used?
questions.h: Think about what causes the variation of the random variable.
questions.answer: When a random variable's variation is the total of a large number of small independent effects
wrong: Only when counting rare independent events in a fixed time interval
Only when sampling without replacement from a small finite population
Only when a variable takes two possible values
questions.e: The Normal distribution is widely used when variation comes from the sum of many small independent effects, and for approximating other distributions.

questions.q: How do you standardize a normal random variable X ~ N(μ, σ²) into Z ~ N(0, 1)?
questions.h: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation (not the variance!).
questions.e: Standardization transforms X ~ N(μ, σ²) via Z = (X - μ) / σ into Z ~ N(0, 1) with E(Z) = 0 and Var(Z) = 1.

questions.q: For Z ~ N(0, 1), how do we find F(-z) from Table I and z_{0.05} from Table II?
questions.h: The standard normal curve is symmetric around zero.
questions.e: Symmetry around 0 gives F(-z) = 1 - F(z) and z_{1-P} = -z_P, so z_{0.05} = -z_{0.95} = -1.645.

questions.q: For Z ~ N(0, 1), given F(1) = 0.84134, what is P(-1 < Z < 1)?
If X ~ N(μ = 10, σ² = 25), what is the 97.5% quantile x_{0.975} (given z_{0.975} = 1.96)?
questions.h: Use x_P = μ + σ·z_P, remembering that σ = √25 = 5.

questions.q: When can Student's t-distribution t(df) be approximated by the standard normal distribution Z ~ N(0, 1)?
questions.h: Classical textbooks give a threshold on the degrees of freedom df.
questions.answer: When df is large enough (classical textbooks: df > 30)
questions.e: When df is large enough (df > 30 in classical textbooks), t_P(df) ≈ z_P. Also, by symmetry around 0, t_{1-P}(df) = -t_P(df).

questions.q: What quantile property holds for the Fisher-Snedecor F-distribution F(df₁, df₂)?
questions.h: Notice that df₁ and df₂ swap places in the reciprocal.
questions.e: For the F-distribution, lower-tail quantiles are obtained from upper-tail quantiles with swapped degrees of freedom: f_{1-P}(df₁, df₂) = 1 / f_P(df₂, df₁).

vocab.meaning: A procedure in which every possible sample of size n has an equal probability of being selected.
Sampling where an element can be selected more than once, keeping trial probabilities constant (independent).
Sampling where an element can be selected at most once, so trial probabilities change (dependent).
Selecting the first element randomly and further elements using a constant skip interval (e.g., every 10th).
Dividing the population into homogeneous strata and drawing a sample from each stratum.
Dividing the population into clusters, randomly selecting some clusters, and surveying all elements in them.
A combination of several sampling methods, often used in practice.
A single-trial binary distribution equivalent to Binomial with n = 1: Bi(1, π).
Models the number of successes in n independent trials, each with success probability π.
Models the number of successes in n dependent trials drawn without replacement from N elements (M successes).
Models the number of random independent occurrences in a continuous interval with average rate λ.
The bell-shaped continuous distribution with mean μ and variance σ², modeling sums of many small independent effects.
The special normal distribution Z with μ = 0 and σ² = 1, tabulated in Tables I and II.
Transforming X ~ N(μ, σ²) into Z = (X - μ) / σ ~ N(0, 1).
A derived continuous distribution parameterized by degrees of freedom df.
A symmetric derived continuous distribution with parameter df; approaches N(0, 1) when df > 30.
A derived continuous distribution with two degrees-of-freedom parameters df₁ and df₂.

facts: In {stratified|cluster|systematic|multistage} sampling, the population is divided into homogeneous groups and samples are taken from every group.
Sampling {without replacement|with replacement|systematically|by cluster} produces dependent random trials.
For X ~ Bi(n, π), the expected value is {n·π|n·π·(1-π)|π|n/π}.
We can approximate Hy(N, M, n) by Bi(n, M/N) when {n < 0.05·N|n > 30|π ≤ 0.1|df > 30}.
For X ~ Po(λ), both E(X) and Var(X) equal {λ|λ²|√λ|1/λ}.
Poisson Po(λ = n·π) approximates Bi(n, π) when π ≤ 0.1 and {n > 30|n < 0.05·N|π = 0.5|n = 1}.
Standardizing X ~ N(μ, σ²) uses Z = {(X - μ) / σ|(X - μ) / σ²|(X + μ) / σ|(μ - X) / σ²}.
For Z ~ N(0, 1), symmetry gives F(-z) = {1 - F(z)|-F(z)|F(z)|1 + F(z)}.
To convert a standard normal quantile z_P back to X ~ N(μ, σ²), compute {μ + σ·z_P|μ + σ²·z_P|μ - σ·z_P|(z_P - μ)/σ}.
Student's t(df) can be approximated by Z ~ N(0, 1) when {df > 30|df < 30|df = 1|π ≤ 0.1}.
For F(df₁, df₂), the lower quantile f_(1-P)(df₁, df₂) equals {1 / f_P(df₂, df₁)|-f_P(df₁, df₂)|1 - f_P(df₁, df₂)|1 / f_P(df₁, df₂)}.
